subChunks.title: READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE
subChunks.hookHtml: Isolation is a spectrum. Higher isolation means fewer concurrency bugs — but also more contention and lower throughput. The right level depends on what your application can tolerate.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The four levels (SQL standard)

LevelDirty ReadNon-repeatable ReadPhantom Read
READ UNCOMMITTEDPossiblePossiblePossible
READ COMMITTEDPreventedPossiblePossible
REPEATABLE READPreventedPreventedPossible (in some)
SERIALIZABLEPreventedPreventedPrevented

Setting isolation level

-- For a transaction:
BEGIN;
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
...
COMMIT;

-- Session default (PostgreSQL):
SET default_transaction_isolation = 'read committed';

READ COMMITTED (PostgreSQL default)

Each statement sees the latest committed rows at statement start. A transaction can see rows committed by other transactions mid-flight. Protects against dirty reads but not non-repeatable reads.

REPEATABLE READ

A transaction sees a snapshot of the database at its start. Other transactions' commits are invisible to it. Protects against non-repeatable reads. PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ also prevents phantoms using MVCC.

SERIALIZABLE

Transactions behave as if they ran one after another, even when concurrent. Highest consistency but most likely to fail with serialisation errors that require retry. Used for financial transactions where correctness is non-negotiable.

MVCC — how PostgreSQL avoids locking

Most locks in PostgreSQL are implemented via MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control): each transaction sees its own snapshot version of rows. Writers do not block readers; readers do not block writers. Only write-write conflicts require actual locking.

storyBeats.text: Two senior archivists are updating different parts of the ledger simultaneously. One sees a stale balance; the other sees a row that will be rolled back.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Isolation levels are a trade-off between correctness and throughput. READ COMMITTED is the practical default — it prevents dirty reads but allows non-repeatable reads. SERIALIZABLE is the strictest — concurrent transactions can fail and must retry. Most applications use READ COMMITTED with explicit locks (SELECT FOR UPDATE) for the specific rows that need stronger guarantees.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Isolation level selection

For each scenario, recommend an isolation level and explain why:

  1. A read-only analytics query that takes 60 seconds to run — during which the underlying data changes
  2. A bank transfer (debit one account, credit another)
  3. A social media application counting post likes
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. REPEATABLE READ — the analytics query should see a consistent snapshot from the moment it starts. Without this, the 60-second query could read some rows from before and some from after another transaction's commit, producing inconsistent aggregates. REPEATABLE READ gives a point-in-time snapshot for the entire transaction.

2. SERIALIZABLE — bank transfers require the strongest guarantee. Any amount being transferred must not be read-then-written by two concurrent transactions. Use SERIALIZABLE and implement retry logic for serialisation failures. Alternatively, use READ COMMITTED + SELECT FOR UPDATE to lock the specific account rows being modified.

3. READ COMMITTED — like counts that are a few milliseconds stale are acceptable. Dirty reads are prevented (preventing a like count from a rolled-back insert), but non-repeatable reads in a 60ms HTTP request are harmless. READ COMMITTED with its lower overhead is appropriate.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Explain what MVCC is and why it allows readers and writers to coexist without blocking each other in PostgreSQL.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) maintains multiple versions of each row. When a transaction updates a row, PostgreSQL does not overwrite the old value — it creates a new row version and marks the old version with the transaction's commit timestamp.

Each transaction sees the version of each row that was current at the transaction's start (or statement start for READ COMMITTED). Readers see old versions; writers create new versions. Since they operate on different versions, readers never block writers and writers never block readers.

Only write-write conflicts (two transactions trying to modify the same row) require actual locking. This is why PostgreSQL handles high concurrency well — the most common operation (reading) never waits for writes.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain READ COMMITTED and SERIALIZABLE isolation levels using a concrete bank transfer example. When would each be appropriate?

questions.prompt: What does READ COMMITTED isolation prevent?
options: Dirty reads — reading uncommitted data from another transaction
questions.answer: Dirty reads — reading uncommitted data from another transaction
questions.explanation: READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads by only showing committed data. It does not prevent non-repeatable reads (the same row might show different values within one transaction if another commits in between).

questions.prompt: Transaction A reads balance=500. Transaction B commits a change making it 600. Transaction A reads again and sees 600. What problem is this?
options: Non-repeatable read — the same row returned different values within the same transaction
Phantom read — a new row appeared in a range query
Lost update — Transaction A's change was overwritten
questions.answer: Non-repeatable read — the same row returned different values within the same transaction
questions.explanation: A non-repeatable read occurs when Transaction A reads the same row twice and gets different values because Transaction B committed a change in between. REPEATABLE READ prevents this by snapshotting data at transaction start.

questions.prompt: When would SERIALIZABLE isolation cause a transaction to fail with an error?
options: When the execution of concurrent transactions cannot be proven equivalent to any serial (one-at-a-time) execution
When two transactions read the same row
When the transaction takes longer than the lock timeout
questions.answer: When the execution of concurrent transactions cannot be proven equivalent to any serial (one-at-a-time) execution
questions.explanation: SERIALIZABLE uses snapshot isolation + serialisation checks. If the engine detects a cycle in the dependency graph of concurrent transactions (indicating a non-serialisable execution), it aborts one transaction with a serialisation failure. Applications must implement retry logic.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, writers do not block readers even under SERIALIZABLE isolation. Why?
options: MVCC — each transaction reads its own snapshot version of rows; old versions remain visible until all transactions that might read them are complete
PostgreSQL uses optimistic locking for all writes
Readers always take priority over writers in PostgreSQL's scheduler
SERIALIZABLE is implemented without locks in PostgreSQL
questions.answer: MVCC — each transaction reads its own snapshot version of rows; old versions remain visible until all transactions that might read them are complete
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL's MVCC keeps old row versions. Readers see the snapshot from their transaction start regardless of concurrent writes. Writers create new versions. This means read and write operations proceed concurrently on the same rows — a key reason PostgreSQL scales well under mixed workloads.
